heading: Introduction
subheading: Who this is for / What is in this part
content:
[Part A | Introduction > Who this is for / What is in this part]

AI Fundamentals

Part A of the company AI training: a beginner's guide to learning AI and bringing it into your daily work

This part is for beginners who are starting to learn AI and want to use AI tools in their daily work. We start from the basics and build up step by step. By the end, you should understand what AI is, how tools like Claude work in simple terms, what they do well, where they go wrong, and how to start using Claude for your own tasks.

Module | Topic | You will practice
----------------------------------
1 | What is AI? | Finding three tasks in your workday where AI could help
2 | What is an LLM? | Asking the same question three times
3 | How does an LLM work? | Seeing what happens when you ask about your company or recent news
4 | Strengths, limits, and trust | Finding something Claude gets wrong
5 | Meet Claude | Completing a first real work task

The document also includes a plain-English glossary, answers to commonly asked questions, and a checklist of what you should be able to do after Part A.

heading: Module 1: What Is AI?
subheading: How the terms fit together
content:
[Part A | Module 1: What Is AI? > How the terms fit together]

AI (Artificial Intelligence) means computer programs that can do tasks that normally need human thinking, such as understanding language, spotting patterns, or making suggestions.

You already use AI every day without noticing:

Your email filters spam.

Your phone suggests the next word as you type.

Streaming apps recommend what to watch.

Maps estimate your travel time.

The AI in this course is different from those. Those tools do one narrow job. The AI we'll learn is a general-purpose assistant: you talk to it in normal language, and it can help with writing, summarizing, explaining, planning, analyzing, and much more.

Term | Plain meaning
--------------------
AI | The big umbrella: computers doing "smart" tasks
Machine learning | A way of building AI where the computer learns from many examples instead of being given step-by-step rules
LLM (Large Language Model) | A type of machine learning built to understand and write human language. Claude is one

Figure 1: Each term sits inside the one before it

Why is this happening now? Three things came together: huge amounts of text available to learn from, much more powerful computers, and better ways of designing these systems.

heading: Module 1: What Is AI?
subheading: A useful way to think about Claude / Common myths
content:
[Part A | Module 1: What Is AI? > A useful way to think about Claude / Common myths]

Imagine a new colleague who has read an enormous amount, works instantly, and is happy to help with almost anything. But they know nothing about your company, your customers, or your project until you tell them, and sometimes they make mistakes. Good results come from explaining things clearly and checking their work.

"It thinks like a human." It doesn't. It works very differently, even if the replies feel natural.

"It's like Google." Google finds existing pages. Claude writes a new answer each time.

"It's always right." It can be wrong, and still sound confident.

"It learns from me instantly." It doesn't change itself during your chat. It only uses what's in the conversation.

Try it: Think of three places in your workday where you spend time on writing, reading, or organizing information. Note them down. We'll come back to them.

heading: Module 2: What Is an LLM?
subheading: Tokens
content:
[Part A | Module 2: What Is an LLM? > Tokens]

An LLM is a program that was trained on a huge amount of text (books, articles, websites, and more) so that it learned how language works and how ideas connect.

The core idea is simple: given some text, an LLM predicts what text should come next. Do this one small piece at a time, very well, and you get full answers, emails, summaries, and explanations.

Think of the way your phone suggests the next word, but vastly more powerful. It has absorbed so many patterns that it can follow instructions, answer questions, and write in different styles.

Figure 2: The LLM weighs several likely next words and picks one

The percentages are examples only, to show the idea.

An LLM doesn't read whole words the way we do. It breaks text into small pieces called tokens (a token can be a word, part of a word, or a punctuation mark). Tokens matter because they set how much text the AI can handle at once and how usage is measured.

heading: Module 2: What Is an LLM?
subheading: Why answers can differ each time
content:
[Part A | Module 2: What Is an LLM? > Why answers can differ each time]

Regular software gives the same result every time you do the same thing. An LLM chooses among likely options, as Figure 2 shows, so asking the same question twice can give two different, equally reasonable answers. This is normal. It's why you should read and judge the output, not treat it as final.

Try it: Ask Claude the same question three times, for example "Give me a short explanation of how to run a good team meeting." Compare the three answers. What stayed the same? What changed?

module: Module 3: How Does an LLM Work?
heading: Module 3: How Does an LLM Work?
content:
[Part A | Module 3: How Does an LLM Work?]

Here is the simple picture in four steps. The first two happen once, before you ever use Claude. The last two happen every time you send a message.

Figure 3: From training to your reply

Step 1: Learning from text (pretraining). The model reads a vast amount of text and learns patterns: grammar, facts, writing styles, how people explain things. This is where most of its general knowledge comes from.

Step 2: Learning to be helpful (fine-tuning and feedback). A model that only predicts text isn't yet a good assistant. It's then further trained, including with feedback from people, so it follows instructions, stays polite, avoids harmful answers, and gives useful replies.

Step 3: You ask a question. Your message is turned into tokens and the model uses everything in the conversation so far to work out a response.

Step 4: It writes the reply piece by piece. It predicts one token at a time until the answer is complete. That's why you often see the reply appear gradually.

module: Module 3: How Does an LLM Work?
heading: Module 3: How Does an LLM Work?
subheading: Three important things to know
content:
[Part A | Module 3: How Does an LLM Work? > Three important things to know]

It has a knowledge cutoff. The model only learned from text up to a certain date. It won't know about anything after that unless it's given a way to search the web or you give it the information.

It doesn't look things up by default. It answers from what it learned, not from a database of verified facts.

Hallucination. Because it generates likely-sounding text, it can sometimes produce details that are false, such as a wrong figure, a made-up source, or an incorrect date, and present them confidently. This is called a hallucination. It's the main reason we always check important information.

Try it: Ask Claude about something very specific to your company or something that happened very recently. Notice what it says. Does it admit it doesn't know, or does it guess? Discuss why.

heading: Module 4: Strengths, Limits, and Trust
subheading: What AI is good at / Where it needs care / Uneven skill / The trust rule: check in proportion to the stakes
content:
[Part A | Module 4: Strengths, Limits, and Trust > What AI is good at / Where it needs care / Uneven skill / The trust rule: check in proportion to the stakes]

Drafting emails, reports, and messages

Rewriting text to be clearer, shorter, or more formal

Summarizing long documents

Explaining difficult topics in simple words

Brainstorming ideas and options

Organizing messy information into tables or lists

Helping with spreadsheets and simple calculations

Exact facts, numbers, dates, and quotes

Precise calculations done "in its head"

Anything it cannot see (a file you didn't share, an event it wasn't told about)

Very recent news

Company-specific details it hasn't been given

AI can be excellent at one task and surprisingly poor at a similar one. Don't assume that doing well in one area means it will do well in another. Try, then check.

Before you rely on an answer, ask one question: what happens if this is wrong? The answer tells you how much to check.

Figure 4: How much to check an AI answer

Situation | How much to check
-----------------------------
Brainstorming, rough drafts | A quick read
Emails, internal notes, numbers, shared reports | Check key facts before sending or sharing
Legal, financial, customer-facing, or sensitive content | Full review, and involve the right expert

Trusting too much leads to mistakes getting through. Trusting too little means you never get the benefit. The goal is balance.

heading: Module 4: Strengths, Limits, and Trust
subheading: Privacy basics
content:
[Part A | Module 4: Strengths, Limits, and Trust > Privacy basics]

Before you start, remember: don't paste passwords, customer personal information, or confidential material into any AI tool unless your company has said it is approved. Follow the company's AI and data policy. We cover this in more depth in Part B.

Try it: Find something Claude gets wrong or handles badly. Share it with the group. Spotting mistakes early builds the right instincts.

heading: Module 5: Meet Claude
subheading: Different models / Ways to use Claude
content:
[Part A | Module 5: Meet Claude > Different models / Ways to use Claude]

Claude is an AI assistant made by Anthropic. It's built on an LLM, so everything in Modules 1 to 4 applies to it.

Claude comes in different versions, called models. Broadly, smaller models are faster and cheaper and suit simple tasks, while larger models are more capable and suit complex ones. You'll learn how to choose in Part B.

Way | What it is | Who it's for
-------------------------------
Claude app (web, desktop, mobile) | Chat with Claude, attach files, get help with everyday work | Everyone
Claude Code | Claude working inside a project, able to read files and take actions | Building and working with AI systems (Part C)
API | A way for software to connect to Claude | Developers building products

heading: Module 5: Meet Claude
subheading: Chat vs. agent / Three habits for good results
content:
[Part A | Module 5: Meet Claude > Chat vs. agent / Three habits for good results]

In a chat, you ask and Claude answers.

With an agent, Claude can also do things: open files, run steps, use tools, and work through a multi-step task. Claude Code works this way. You will learn more about agents in Part B.

Figure 5: Chat compared with an agent

Give context. Say who you are, what the situation is, and who the output is for.

State the goal. Say clearly what you want.

Ask for the format. For example "a short email," "a table," or "five bullet points."

Weak request: "Write something about the meeting change."

Better request: "I'm a team lead. Write a short email to my team of 10 explaining that our weekly meeting is moving from Monday to Tuesday at 10 am, starting next week. Keep it friendly and under 80 words."

Try it (first real task): Pick one of the three work tasks you noted in Module 1. Use Claude to help with it. Afterward, note what worked, what didn't, and what you would do differently next time.

heading: Glossary: AI Terms in Plain English
content:
[Part A | Glossary]

Part B will add more terms: reasoning models, agents, permissions, skills, memory, and harness.

Term | Plain meaning
--------------------
AI (Artificial Intelligence) | Computer programs that do tasks that normally need human thinking
Machine learning | Teaching a computer by showing it many examples, instead of writing rules for everything
Model | The trained "brain" of an AI system. Claude is made up of models
LLM (Large Language Model) | A model trained on huge amounts of text so it can understand and write language
Training | The process of teaching a model by having it learn from large amounts of data
Prompt | What you type to the AI: your question, request, or instructions
Token | A small piece of text (a word or part of a word) that the AI reads and writes
Response / output | The reply the AI gives you
Context | Everything the AI can see during your conversation: your messages, its replies, and any files you shared

heading: Glossary: AI Terms in Plain English
content:
[Part A | Glossary]

Term | Plain meaning
--------------------
Context window | The limit on how much the AI can hold in view at once, like the size of its desk
Hallucination | When the AI states something false or made up, but sounds confident
Knowledge cutoff | The date after which the AI has not learned anything new
Fine-tuning | Extra training that shapes a model to behave in a particular way
Agent | An AI that doesn't only answer but also takes actions and works through steps using tools
Tool | Something the AI can use to do more than write text, such as searching the web or reading a file
Multimodal | Able to work with more than text, such as images and documents
API | A way for one piece of software to talk to another. Companies use Claude's API to build it into their own tools

heading: Commonly Asked Questions
subheading: Understanding AI / How it behaves
content:
[Part A | FAQ > Understanding AI / How it behaves]

1. Is AI actually intelligent?

It's very good at working with language and patterns, but it doesn't think or understand like a person. Treat it as a powerful tool with its own strengths and weaknesses.

2. What's the difference between AI, machine learning, and an LLM?

AI is the whole field. Machine learning is AI that learns from examples. An LLM is a machine learning model specialized in language.

3. Is Claude the same as Google?

No. Google finds existing web pages. Claude writes a new answer based on what it learned and what you tell it.

4. Why does it give different answers to the same question?

It picks among likely responses, so there's some natural variation. Use this to your advantage by asking for a few options.

5. Why does it sometimes make things up?

It generates text that sounds right, not text that is checked against facts. When it lacks information, it may fill the gap with a guess. Always verify important facts.

6. Does it know today's news?

Not on its own. Its knowledge stops at a cutoff date. It can use current information only if it has a search tool or you provide the material.

7. Does it remember my earlier chats?

By default, a new conversation starts fresh. Memory features exist and we cover them in Part B.

8. Does it learn from what I type?

heading: Commonly Asked Questions
subheading: How it behaves / Using it well / Safety
content:
[Part A | FAQ > How it behaves / Using it well]

It doesn't change itself during your chat. It uses what you've said within that conversation. For how data is handled beyond that, follow your company's policy.

9. How do I know if an answer is correct?

Check in proportion to the stakes. A rough draft needs a quick read. Numbers, reports, and customer-facing content need verification against the real source.

10. Why is it sometimes bad at math?

It predicts text rather than calculating. It's more reliable when it uses a tool, such as running a calculation, and when you double-check results.

11. Do I need to write perfect prompts?

No. Give context, state your goal, and say what format you want. If the first answer isn't right, reply with what to change. It's a conversation.

12. What should I do if the answer isn't what I wanted?

Tell Claude what's missing or wrong, for example "Make it shorter," "Use a more formal tone," or "You missed the deadline." Refining is normal and expected.

13. Which model should I use?

Smaller, faster models for simple tasks and larger ones for complex work. Part B covers this properly.

14. What can I paste into Claude?

Follow your company policy. By default, don't paste passwords, customer personal data, or confidential material unless it's been approved.

15. Can it be wrong and still sound sure?

Yes. A confident tone is not proof of accuracy, which is why we check important output.

heading: What You Should Be Able to Do After Part A
content:
[Part A | Checklist]

Explain in simple words what AI and an LLM are

Describe, at a basic level, how Claude produces an answer

Understand why answers vary and why mistakes happen

Decide which tasks suit AI and how carefully to check the results

Know the basic privacy rule

Tell the difference between a chat and an agent

Write a clear request using the three habits: context, goal, and format

Use Claude on a real work task with a clear, well-structured request

Understand the key AI terms in everyday language

heading: Introduction
subheading: Who this is for
content:
[Part B | Introduction > Who this is for]

AI Concepts for Working with AI Systems

Part B of the company AI training: the building blocks behind tools like Claude

This part is for anyone who has finished Part A. Here we explain eight ideas that sit behind every AI tool you will use: which model to pick, what Claude can see, how to ask, how Claude keeps information between chats, how to save a good method, how Claude does real work, how Claude carries out a whole job on its own, and how you keep it safe. The first five modules are about getting good answers in a conversation. The last three are about Claude doing work for you, and keeping that work safe.

Every idea is explained in plain English with a simple everyday example. This part is for understanding. The hands-on practice comes next, in Part C, where you will use these ideas in a small project.

heading: Introduction
subheading: What is in this part / How to read the examples
content:
[Part B | Introduction > What is in this part]

Module | Topic | The big idea
-----------------------------
6 | Types of models | Pick the right model for the task
7 | Context | Claude only knows what is in front of it
8 | Prompting | A clear request gets a better answer
9 | Memory | How Claude keeps information between chats
10 | Skills | Save a good method and reuse it
11 | Tools and the harness | How Claude does work, not only talks
12 | Agents | How Claude works through a whole job, step by step
13 | Permissions and safety | You decide what Claude may open, change, or send

After the eight modules, a worked example shows all eight ideas working together. The document ends with a glossary of new terms, commonly asked questions, and a checklist of what you should be able to explain.

Gray boxes marked Example show a small, realistic situation. Blue boxes marked Remember give the one or two points to keep. Our examples follow Asha, a team lead who is learning to use Claude for everyday work.

heading: Module 6: Types of Models
subheading: Model tiers: small, medium, and large
content:
[Part B | Module 6: Types of Models > Model tiers: small, medium, and large]

In Part A you learned that a model is the trained "brain" behind an AI tool. Claude is not one single model. It is a family of models, and you can choose between them.

Think of hiring help. You would not ask a senior specialist to sort the mailbox, and you would not ask a trainee to review a complex contract. AI models work the same way. Models come in tiers, from smaller and faster to larger and more capable.

Tier | Good for | Trade-off
---------------------------
Smaller and faster | Quick edits, sorting, simple questions, short summaries | Less depth on complex problems
Balanced (mid-range) | Most everyday work: drafting, analysis, spreadsheets | A sensible middle ground
Most capable | Hard, multi-step, or high-stakes tasks | Slower and costs more to run

Claude's models are named by tier (for example Haiku, Sonnet, and Opus, with newer versions released regularly), so check which ones are available to you.

Example: Asha wants to fix typos in a short email. A smaller, faster model is perfect. Later she needs to compare three quotes for a team event and point out the differences. That is a job for a more capable model.

heading: Module 6: Types of Models
subheading: Standard models and thinking (reasoning) models
content:
[Part B | Module 6: Types of Models > Standard models and thinking (reasoning) models]

A standard model answers straight away, like answering a question off the top of your head. A reasoning or thinking model works through the problem step by step first, like working it out on paper before giving the answer. It takes longer and uses more of your allowance, but it does better on hard problems such as detailed analysis, planning, and tricky logic.

Many Claude models can be asked to think before answering. In the Claude app this is usually a setting you can switch on when a task is hard.

Example: "Which supplier quote is cheaper once discounts and tax are included?" A thinking model works through each step and is less likely to slip. "Rewrite this sentence to sound friendlier" does not need thinking at all.

Thinking does not guarantee a correct answer. Keep checking important results, as you learned in Part A.

Figure 6: A simple way to choose a model

heading: Module 6: Types of Models
subheading: Models that can see: multimodal
content:
[Part B | Module 6: Types of Models > Models that can see: multimodal]

Multimodal models work with more than text. You can give Claude a photo of a whiteboard, a chart, a scanned form, or a PDF, and ask questions about it.

Example: Asha photographs the whiteboard after a planning meeting and asks Claude to turn it into a typed action list with owners.

Remember: Match the model to the task. Start with a balanced model, move to a smaller one for simple jobs, and use a more capable one or turn on thinking when the task is hard. Bigger is not always better.

heading: Module 7: Context
subheading: The desk idea
content:
[Part B | Module 7: Context > The desk idea]

Context is everything Claude can see at the moment it answers you. This is one of the most important ideas in the whole course, because Claude can only work with what is in its context.

Picture Claude sitting at a desk. Only the papers on the desk are available to it. The desk holds four kinds of things:

Your instructions: what you asked for

The conversation so far: your earlier messages and Claude's replies

Files you shared: documents, spreadsheets, images

Tool results: information Claude fetched, such as a web search result (more in Module 11)

Figure 7: Claude can only work with what is on its desk

Anything not on the desk does not exist for Claude. It cannot see your company's internal documents, your other chats, or a file you forgot to attach.

Example: Asha types: "Summarize yesterday's meeting." Claude cannot do it, because the meeting notes are not on the desk. She attaches the notes and asks again, and now Claude can help.

heading: Module 7: Context
subheading: The desk has a size limit / Quality matters more than quantity
content:
[Part B | Module 7: Context > The desk has a size limit / Quality matters more than quantity]

The context window is the size of the desk. It is large, but it is not endless. In a very long conversation, or with very large files, the desk fills up. When that happens, Claude may lose track of earlier details, repeat itself, or become less accurate.

A small, relevant desk beats a huge, messy one. If you paste an 80-page report when only two pages matter, you are making Claude search through clutter.

Start a new chat for each new task instead of continuing one long chat.

Share only the files and pages that matter.

In a long chat, ask Claude to summarize what you have agreed, then continue in a fresh chat.

Remember: Claude knows only what is in its context. If an answer is wrong because information was missing, the fix is usually to give it the missing information.

heading: Module 8: Prompting and Instructions
subheading: Four parts of a good request
content:
[Part B | Module 8: Prompting and Instructions > Four parts of a good request]

A prompt is what you type to Claude. Prompting simply means asking clearly. You do not need special tricks. You need to give Claude what a new colleague would need in order to help you.

Figure 8: The four parts of a good request

Part | What to include
----------------------
Situation | Who you are and what is going on
Goal | Exactly what you want Claude to produce
Background | Facts, files, or earlier decisions Claude needs
Format | Length, structure, tone, and who the reader is

Weak request: "Summarize this."

Better request: "I'm preparing for a client meeting tomorrow. Summarize the attached report in five bullet points, focusing on risks and costs. Keep each point under 20 words."

heading: Module 8: Prompting and Instructions
subheading: Other useful techniques
content:
[Part B | Module 8: Prompting and Instructions > Other useful techniques]

Show an example. "Write it in the same style as this email," and paste one. A sample teaches Claude faster than a long description.

Set boundaries. "Don't use jargon," or "If a figure is missing, say so instead of guessing."

Break big jobs into steps. Ask for an outline first, approve it, then ask for the full draft.

Let Claude ask you. "Before you start, ask me up to three questions if anything is unclear."

Refine in follow-ups. The first answer is a draft. Say what to change: "Shorter," "More formal," or "You missed the deadline."

Example: Asha asks for a reminder email. The first draft is too long, so she replies: "Cut this to three sentences and make the deadline stand out." The second draft is what she needed.

Remember: Give situation, goal, background, and format. A few extra sentences at the start save many corrections later.

heading: Module 9: Memory
subheading: Claude does not remember by default / Short-term and saved memory
content:
[Part B | Module 9: Memory > Claude does not remember by default / Short-term and saved memory]

Imagine a colleague who wakes up every morning with no memory of yesterday. To work with them, you would leave a notebook they read first each day. That is how Claude's memory works.

Each new conversation starts fresh. Claude does not carry over what you discussed last week unless something is saved for it to read. This is why the context from Module 7 ends when the chat ends.

Kind | What it is
-----------------
Short-term | The current conversation (the context). It is gone when the chat ends
Saved (persistent) | Notes stored somewhere Claude reads again at the start of future chats

Figure 9: Saved notes are read at the start of each new chat

Saved memory can take a few forms, depending on the tool you use:

Memory feature in the Claude app, where available, which keeps useful details from your chats. You can review and edit it.

Project instructions: standing notes attached to a project that Claude reads every time you work in it.

An instruction file in a project folder (used in Claude Code), which Claude reads at the start of each session.

Example: Asha saves this note: "I'm a team lead. Reports should be short bullet points with no jargon. Dates are written as day, month, year. The weekly report goes out on Fridays." Now every new chat starts with that background, and she doesn't repeat it.

heading: Module 9: Memory
subheading: What to store and what not to store
content:
[Part B | Module 9: Memory > What to store and what not to store]

Good to store: your role, preferences, team conventions, standard wording, key background.

Never store: passwords, customer personal data, or confidential material. Follow company policy.

Keep it tidy. Old or wrong notes lead to wrong answers, so review them from time to time. Memory is not Claude "learning". It is saved notes that Claude reads, and you stay in control of them.

Remember: Claude starts each chat blank. Saved notes are how you give it lasting background. Store preferences, not secrets.

heading: Module 10: Skills
subheading: What a skill is / Skill vs. prompt
content:
[Part B | Module 10: Skills > What a skill is / Skill vs. prompt]

Think about a recipe card. Once you have a good recipe, you don't work out the steps again each time you cook. A skill is a recipe card for Claude.

A skill is a saved set of instructions for one kind of task, often with a template or example attached. It tells Claude how to do that task your way: the steps, the format, the tone, and a checklist to finish with.

Example: Asha writes a weekly status report every Friday. She saves a "weekly report" skill that holds her report template, the order of sections, the tone she likes, and a final checklist. Now she only says, "Write this week's report," and Claude follows the saved method.

Figure 10: A prompt is typed each time, a skill is saved once

 | Prompt | Skill
-----------------
What it is | A one-time request | A saved, reusable method
Effort | You explain it each time | You write it once
Consistency | Can vary between people | Same approach every time
Sharing | Hard to pass on | Easy to share with a team

heading: Module 10: Skills
subheading: How skills stay efficient / When to make a skill
content:
[Part B | Module 10: Skills > How skills stay efficient / When to make a skill]

Claude can see a short description of each skill, and it opens the full instructions only when the task fits. This keeps the desk (the context from Module 7) free of clutter until a skill is actually needed.

You find yourself giving the same instructions again and again.

The output must follow a fixed format or standard.

Several people should do the task the same way.

Keep a skill short and clear, and update it when the method changes. A skill that one person writes well can help the whole team.

Remember: If you explain the same task to Claude more than a few times, turn it into a skill.

heading: Module 11: Tools and the Harness
subheading: Tools: the model's hands / The harness: the whole workshop
content:
[Part B | Module 11: Tools and the Harness > Tools: the model's hands / The harness: the whole workshop]

So far Claude has been writing text. But Claude can also do things, such as read a file, search the web, make a document, or check a calculation. This module explains how.

A model on its own is like a very clever person in a locked room who can only pass notes out under the door. It can think and write, but it cannot open a file or look something up. Tools are what let it reach out: reading a spreadsheet, searching the web, creating a document, or running a calculation.

The harness is the software wrapped around the model. It gives the model its tools, runs the working loop, and enforces the rules about what the model may do. The Claude app is one harness. Claude Code, which you will use later in the course, is another.

Figure 11: The model works inside a harness that gives it tools and rules

This is why the same model can behave differently in different places. The brain is the same, but the tools and rules around it are not.

heading: Module 11: Tools and the Harness
subheading: From tools to agents / One more term you will meet
content:
[Part B | Module 11: Tools and the Harness > From tools to agents / One more term you will meet]

When Claude uses its tools in a loop to finish a whole job, it is working as an agent (Module 12). The rules about what it may open, change, or send are its permissions (Module 13).

A connector links Claude to another app, such as your email or calendar, if you allow it.

Remember: The model thinks. Tools let it act. The harness provides the tools and the rules. You decide what Claude is allowed to do.

heading: Module 12: Agents
subheading: Chat or agent?
content:
[Part B | Module 12: Agents > Chat or agent?]

In Module 11 you saw that tools let Claude do things. An agent is what you get when Claude uses those tools on its own to finish a whole job, not just to answer one question.

Think about the difference between asking a colleague a question and handing a colleague a task. In a chat, you ask and Claude answers, and you decide what happens next. With an agent, you give a goal. Claude decides the steps, uses tools to carry them out, checks its own work, and keeps going until the job is done.

 | Chat | Agent
---------------
You give | A question or a request | A goal
Who decides the next step | You | Claude
What comes back | An answer to read | Finished work, such as a file or a set of changes
Your role | Guide every step | Set the goal and the limits, then review the result

Both use the same model. The difference is how much the harness lets Claude do on its own.

heading: Module 12: Agents
subheading: The agent loop / When an agent helps
content:
[Part B | Module 12: Agents > The agent loop / When an agent helps]

When Claude works as an agent, it repeats a loop: think, act, check the result, repeat until the job is done. It stops when the goal is met, or when it needs your help or your approval.

Figure 12: An agent repeats think, act, check until the job is done

Example: Asha asks: "Find the three most common complaints in this feedback list and write a short note about them." Claude opens the file (tool), counts the comments in each group and checks the numbers (tool), writes the note, then reads it back to confirm it matches the data.

Jobs with several steps, such as gathering information, organizing it, and writing it up.

Work across many files or pages, such as checking 20 documents against one checklist.

Repetitive jobs, such as filling in the same template for each item on a list.

For a quick question, a rewrite, or a brainstorm, a normal chat is simpler and faster. An agent takes more time and uses more of your allowance, so save it for jobs that need several steps.

heading: Module 12: Agents
subheading: Where agents need care / Giving an agent a good goal
content:
[Part B | Module 12: Agents > Where agents need care / Giving an agent a good goal]

A wrong step early on can carry through every step after it, so the final result can look neat and still be wrong.

A vague goal gives a vague result. The agent fills the gaps with guesses.

Agents can change files or send messages, so they need clear limits. You set these with permissions (Module 13).

You are still responsible for the result. Review it before you use or share it.

A goal for an agent works like a good request in Module 8, with two additions: a clear finish line and clear limits. Include these four things:

Goal: what the finished job looks like.

Where to work: which files or folder to use.

Limits: what it must not touch or change.

Check-ins: when it should stop and show you something before going on.

Weak request: "Clean up the reports folder."

Better request: "In the Reports folder, find every file with 'draft' in its name and list them in a table with the date each was last changed. Do not delete or rename anything. Show me the list before you do anything else."

heading: Module 12: Agents
subheading: Subagents: helpers for big jobs / Staying in control
content:
[Part B | Module 12: Agents > Subagents: helpers for big jobs / Staying in control]

A subagent is a helper that Claude starts to handle one part of a larger job. Each subagent works on its own, with its own fresh desk (Module 7), and sends back a short result. This keeps Claude's main desk free of clutter, and some parts of the job can be done side by side.

Example: Asha asks Claude to go through 15 sets of meeting notes and list every action item. Claude starts a helper for each set of notes. Each helper reads one set and sends back a three-line summary of its action items. Claude then combines the 15 summaries into one list for Asha to check.

Start with a small job to see how the agent behaves before giving it a big one.

Say when you want it to check in, for example: "Show me your plan before you start."

Look at the steps it took, not only the final answer.

Use permissions to limit what it can read, change, or send.

Remember: An agent turns a goal into finished work by thinking, acting, and checking in a loop. Give it a clear goal and clear limits, and always review the result.

heading: Module 13: Permissions and Safety
subheading: Why permissions matter
content:
[Part B | Module 13: Permissions and Safety > Why permissions matter]

Claude can only do what its harness allows. Permissions are the rules you set about what Claude may read, change, or send. They are what keep you in control when Claude works as an agent.

Think about giving a new colleague keys to the office. You would give them the key to the rooms they need, not a master key to every room. Permissions work the same way. The idea is to give Claude only the access the job needs. This is called least access.

This matters most when Claude can act, not only talk. An agent can open files, change them, delete them, or send messages. Permissions decide which of these it may do freely, which need your approval, and which it must never do.

heading: Module 13: Permissions and Safety
subheading: Three settings: allow, ask, deny / Keeping Claude away from sensitive files
content:
[Part B | Module 13: Permissions and Safety > Three settings: allow, ask, deny / Keeping Claude away from sensitive files]

Setting | What it means | Everyday example
------------------------------------------
Allow | Claude may do it without asking you | Reading the documents in your project folder
Ask | Claude must stop and wait for your approval each time | Saving over a file, deleting a file, or sending a message
Deny | Claude is never allowed to do it | Opening a file that holds passwords, or a folder of personal data

If rules disagree, the stricter one wins: deny beats ask, and ask beats allow.

Figure 13: Each action is checked against your rules: allow, ask, or deny

Some files should stay out of Claude's reach. A common one is a file named .env (said "dot env"). Software teams use it to store passwords and secret keys that let a program connect to other services. Claude almost never needs to read it, so it is a good file to deny.

You can do the same for other sensitive material, such as:

Folders with customer personal data.

Payroll, HR, or salary files.

Signed contracts and legal files.

Anything that holds passwords, keys, or access codes.

When a file is denied, Claude cannot open it. If a task needs that file, Claude tells you it does not have access instead of reading it.

heading: Module 13: Permissions and Safety
subheading: Keeping Claude away from sensitive files / How to set it up in Claude Code

heading: Module 13: Permissions and Safety
subheading: Approval prompts: read before you click / Permissions in the Claude app / Good habits
content:
[Part B | Module 13: Permissions and Safety > Approval prompts: read before you click / Permissions in the Claude app / Good habits]

When a setting is "ask", Claude stops and shows you what it wants to do. Read it before you approve. Many tools also offer to remember your answer. Choose that only for actions you are happy to allow every time, such as reading documents, and never for deleting or sending.

In the Claude app, the same idea applies to connectors (Module 11). When you connect an app such as your email or calendar, you choose what Claude may do with it. For example, Claude may read your calendar, but ask before sending an email. You can disconnect an app at any time.

Start strict and loosen later. It is easier to allow more than to undo a mistake.

Deny access to secrets and personal data before you start.

Read every approval prompt for changing, deleting, or sending.

Work on a copy of important files, so the original is safe.

Never paste passwords or confidential material into a chat. Follow your company's data policy.

Remember: Permissions decide what Claude may do on its own. Allow what is safe, ask for what matters, and deny what is sensitive, such as an .env file. You stay responsible for the result.

heading: Putting It All Together
content:
[Part B | Worked Example]

Here is how the eight ideas work together in one everyday job: a weekly status report assistant for Asha's team.

Figure 14: The ideas from Modules 6 to 13 in one picture

Idea | How it appears in the example
------------------------------------
Model (Module 6) | A balanced model is enough for drafting. Thinking is switched on only if the numbers need careful checking
Context (Module 7) | Asha gives it this week's task list and last week's report, and nothing else
Prompt (Module 8) | "I'm the team lead. Write this week's status report as five short bullet points for senior management."
Memory (Module 9) | A saved note holds Asha's role, her team's preferences, and who receives the report
Skill (Module 10) | A "weekly report" skill holds the template, section order, tone, and checklist
Tools and harness (Module 11) | Claude reads the task file, checks the totals with a calculation, and creates the document
Agent (Module 12) | Claude works through the job as an agent: it reads the task list, checks the totals, writes the report, and compares it with the list before stopping for Asha's review
Permissions (Module 13) | Claude may read the team folder and must ask before saving anything. The payroll folder and any file holding passwords are denied

Notice that no single idea does the job alone. A good result comes from choosing the right model, giving it the right context, asking clearly, keeping useful notes, reusing a saved method, and letting it work as an agent within clear permissions. In Part C you will build a small project like this yourself.

heading: Glossary: New Terms in Plain English
content:
[Part B | Glossary]

Terms from Part A, such as model, prompt, token, context, and hallucination, are in the Part A glossary.

Term | Plain meaning
--------------------
Model tier | A version of the model, from small and fast to large and capable
Reasoning (thinking) model | A model that works through a problem step by step before it answers
Prompting | The skill of asking Claude clearly so you get a useful answer
Memory | Information saved so Claude can use it again in later conversations
Project instructions | Standing notes attached to a project that Claude reads each time you work in it
Skill | A saved set of instructions, often with a template, for a repeatable task
Harness | The software around the model that gives it tools, runs its working loop, and enforces rules
Connector | A link that lets Claude read from or act in another app, such as email or a calendar
Agent | An AI that works toward a goal in steps, using tools, until the job is done

heading: Glossary: New Terms in Plain English
content:
[Part B | Glossary]

Term | Plain meaning
--------------------
Agent loop | The cycle of thinking, acting with a tool, checking the result, and repeating
Subagent | A helper Claude starts to handle one part of a larger job
Permission | A setting that controls what Claude may do on its own and what needs your approval
Allow, ask, deny | The three permission settings: do it freely, stop and ask me first, or never do it
Deny rule | A rule that blocks Claude from using a file, folder, or action, such as a file that holds passwords
Approval prompt | A message where Claude stops and asks for your OK before it acts
Least access | Giving Claude only the access the job needs, and nothing more
.env file | A file that holds the passwords and secret keys a program uses to connect to other services

heading: Commonly Asked Questions
subheading: Models / Context and prompts
content:
[Part B | FAQ > Models / Context and prompts]

1. Is the biggest model always the best choice?

No. Larger models are slower and cost more. For simple tasks, a smaller model is just as good and much faster.

2. What does "thinking" actually do?

The model spends extra time working through the problem before it replies. It helps on hard tasks and is wasted effort on easy ones.

3. If thinking is on, can I trust the answer without checking?

No. Thinking improves the odds of a good answer, but it does not make Claude always right. Check important results.

4. Can Claude read images and PDFs?

Yes. Multimodal models can work with images, charts, and documents, not only typed text.

5. Why does Claude seem to forget things in a long chat?

The context window has a limit, and very long chats crowd it. Start a new chat and paste a short summary of what matters.

6. Is a longer prompt always a better prompt?

No. Relevant detail helps. Long, unfocused detail makes it harder for Claude to find what matters.

7. Do I have to repeat my background in every new chat?

Not if you save it. Memory and project instructions (Module 9) carry your background into new chats.

heading: Commonly Asked Questions
subheading: Memory and skills / Tools, agents, and permissions
content:
[Part B | FAQ > Memory and skills / Tools, agents, and permissions]

8. Does memory mean Claude is learning from me?

No. Memory is saved notes that Claude reads at the start of a chat. The model itself does not change.

9. What should I never save in memory?

Passwords, customer personal data, and confidential material. Follow your company's data policy.

10. Is a skill the same as a prompt?

A prompt is a one-time request. A skill is a saved, reusable method that Claude can use whenever the task fits.

11. What is the difference between the Claude app and Claude Code?

They use the same family of models but have different harnesses. Claude Code is built to work inside a project and take actions with files and tools.

12. Can Claude open my files or email by itself?

Only if you share them or connect the app, and you control the permissions. Without access, it cannot see them.

13. Who is responsible if Claude makes a mistake while acting?

You are. That is why permissions exist and why you review the results, especially before anything is sent, saved, or shared.

14. What is the difference between a chatbot and an agent?

In a chat, you ask and Claude answers. An agent is given a goal and works through the steps itself, using tools, until the job is done. See Module 12.

15. When should I use an agent instead of a normal chat?

heading: Commonly Asked Questions
subheading: Tools, agents, and permissions
content:
[Part B | FAQ > Tools, agents, and permissions]

Use an agent for jobs with several steps or many files. Use a normal chat for quick questions, rewrites, and brainstorming.

16. Can an agent make mistakes along the way?

Yes. A wrong early step can carry into later steps. Give a clear goal, ask it to show its plan or steps, and review the result.

17. Can I stop Claude from reading a particular file, such as a .env file?

Yes. In Claude Code, add a deny rule for that file or folder, for example "Read(./.env)" in the permissions section of the project settings. Claude then cannot open it. See Module 13.

18. What is the difference between "ask" and "deny"?

With "ask", Claude stops and waits for your approval each time. With "deny", Claude is never allowed to do it. If rules disagree, the stricter one wins.

19. If I deny a file, is it completely safe?

A deny rule is one layer of protection, not the only one. Keep real passwords out of shared project folders where you can, and follow your company's security guidance.

content:

Choose a suitable model for a simple task and for a hard one

Explain what context is and why Claude can only work with what it can see

Write a request with a situation, goal, background, and format

Explain how memory works, what to save, and what never to save

Describe what a skill is and when to create one

Explain what a tool and a harness are, and why the same model can behave differently in different places

Explain what an agent is, how the agent loop works, and what a subagent does

Give an agent a clear goal with limits and check-ins

Explain allow, ask, and deny, and how to keep Claude away from sensitive files such as an .env file

Describe how all eight ideas work together in one task
